claims.text: **The facts hold up.** Google paid $250,000 for a three-bug Chrome chain that XBOW built from August 2–7, 2026, using `gpt-5.6-sol` agents.
XBOW reconstructed about $40,000 of API charges from archived Codex logs [^1,2].
Dolan-Gavitt's pre-LLM baseline is a team of four for 6–9 months, roughly 24–36 researcher-months.
The same capability sells for $2–3M to brokers [^10] and at most $250K from Google.
Google has already cut bounties on the bug classes AI finds cheaply [^13].
XBOW CEO Oege de Moor's announcement says Google awarded $250,000, "the first under its 2026 new rules," and that the bugs "are now fixed" [^1].
The companion technical post by Brendan Dolan-Gavitt names the parts at component level: "a V8 compiler bug, an animated-WebP decoder bug, and a memory-safety bug in Crashpad" [^2].
The August 25 desktop stable update lists CVE-2026-78952, a High-severity out-of-bounds write in Crashpad reported by Dolan-Gavitt of XBOW on August 13 [^5,7].
The September 3 update lists CVE-2026-85045, a High-severity race condition in V8 reported by Dolan-Gavitt on August 17 [^4,6].
XBOW's press release, and coverage that copied it, puts CVE-2026-85045 on the WebP bug [^3,32].
Its Chromium issue ID matches the one XBOW's own technical post gives for the Maglev bug [^4,6].
A first full chain "died when its final stage collided with a bug that had been found internally by Google months before" [^2].
A widely shared social post claimed six.
Google's own 2025 year-in-review lists a $250,000 top reward for 2025 [^11].
SecurityWeek reported a $250,000 payout for a Chrome Mojo sandbox escape (CVE-2025-4609) in August 2025 [^16].
The two public CVEs are independently verifiable, the fixes shipped within 12 and 17 days of report
$40,000 against $250,000 is 16 cents of compute per bounty dollar.
Dolan-Gavitt's sentence is precise: "Reconstructing usage from the archived Codex logs puts the six-day campaign at roughly $40,000 in API charges" [^2].
The US Bureau of Labor Statistics puts the median annual wage for information security analysts at $129,180 as of May 2025, about $10,765 a month [^31].
At that floor, Dolan-Gavitt's pre-LLM baseline of 24–36 researcher-months costs about $258K–$388K in wages alone [^2,31].
Four researchers from January to August is up to about 28 researcher-months, or about $300K at the median wage [^1,31].
XBOW's credits include a $1,000 Blink bug reported in July [^5].
Dolan-Gavitt's own timeline is unusually candid: "Pre-LLMs a Chrome full chain would take a team of four around 6-9 months to be produced

De Moor cites a different anchor, a former intelligence-agency staffer who said his team "used to spend six months trying to identify this kind of vulnerability and get total access. We did it in six days" [^1].
At the low end of the baseline (four people, six months), the labor input is about 104 researcher-weeks.
OpenAI's system card treats GPT-5.6 Sol as High capability in cybersecurity under its Preparedness Framework, below Critical [^20,21].

Summaries of OpenAI's Chromium and Firefox evaluations say the models found bugs and exploitation primitives but "could not autonomously chain those primitives into a complete, functional exploit" [^21].
XBOW's own forecast, that "within a year, each of the three bugs could be found by agents working on their own," is a prediction, not data [^1].
GPT-5.6 Sol shipped generally on July 9, 2026, at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output tokens [^19,20].
OpenAI's model page now lists $4 input, $0.40 cached input and $20 output, "available at least through November 21, 2026" [^18,19].
Long prompts above 272K input tokens are billed at 2× input and 1.5× output for the whole request [^18].
In a July 14 lab benchmark, GPT-5.6 Sol Ultra built a working V8 exploit from public security-fix commits for $1,596.89 of compute.
The root agent consumed 819.6 million input tokens, and 74 subagents together processed 1.27 billion input tokens and 4.04 million output tokens [^22,23].
At Hacktron's blended rate, $40,000 corresponds to on the order of 50 billion tokens.
Hacktron's run was an **n-day** renderer exploit with the patch commit as a map, in a sandboxed test build, with "limited guidance" [^22,23].
Anthropic's sub-$2,000 kernel chain was also n-day work, and its OpenBSD figure covers a thousand runs of *search* [^24].
Trail of Bits' $39.6K bought 28 vulnerabilities and 19 patches across a whole competition, not one exploit [^27].

In April 2024 Crowdfense advertised a $30 million acquisition program that would pay "between $2 million and $3 million for Chrome exploits leading to remote code execution and local privilege escalation" [^10].
Google's top Chrome tier has risen from up to $180,000 for the first full chain in a temporary 2023 offer [^15] to $250,000 since its August 2024 restructure.
Pwn2Own Berlin 2026 priced a Chrome sandbox escape at $175,000 [^17].
On these numbers, Google's full-chain bounty is about 8–12% of the advertised broker price for comparable impact [^10,1].
Some former exploit developers have said Crowdfense's Chrome prices were *below* market [^10].

In its spring 2026 revision Google cut the Chrome memory-safety base reward to $500 with multipliers, and phased out the bonuses for arbitrary read/write and renderer RCE introduced the year before [^9,13].
It explicitly prioritized "categories that remain more challenging for automated AI tooling to find" [^8].
Chrome Security's Q2 2026 summary says the reward structure was adjusted "to reflect the volume of reports being discovered and fixed using internal AI tooling".
Google paid a record $17.1 million across all programs in 2025, to 747 researchers, more than 40% above 2024 [^11,13].
Chrome's VRP paid $3,716,750 in 2025 against $3.4 million to 137 researchers for 337 valid bugs in 2024 [^12,13].
On 2025 numbers, XBOW's single award equals about 6.7% of the entire Chrome VRP year [^13,1].
SecurityWeek has since linked to a story headlined "Google Partially Reverses Chrome Bug Bounty Cuts," which we could not retrieve, so the base-reward figures may have moved since May [^9].
Two and a half years ago, a University of Illinois team reported that GPT-4 could exploit 87% of a set of 15 one-day vulnerabilities when given the CVE description, versus 7% without it [^28].
It estimated about $8.80 per successful exploit at $10/$30 per million tokens [^28].
Those were web-application one-days, with the CVE text as a map.
In April 2026, Anthropic reported Mythos Preview producing Linux kernel n-day chains for under $2,000.
Google Threat Intelligence Group tracked 90 in-the-wild zero-days in 2025, up from 78 in 2024 and below 2023's record 100.
XBOW raised a $120 million Series C on March 18, 2026, at a valuation over $1 billion, led by DFJ Growth and Northzone [^29].
It had previously reached the top of HackerOne's US leaderboard in 2025, submitting nearly 1,060 vulnerabilities.
Bug bounty programs had resolved 130 of them, with 303 triaged, 208 duplicates and 209 informative at the time of its post [^30,25].
De Moor's post closes by inviting design partners for "an autonomous product for testing compiled software" [^1].
That supports its decision to ship Sol broadly behind classifiers rather than restrict it [^20,21].

We could not locate a public CVE for the WebP stage, could not read OpenAI's system-card PDF directly (it is cited through third-party summaries), and could not verify XBOW's claim that this was only the second $250K full-chain award in Chrome's history.
Its researchers built the chain in six days in Las Vegas with AI agents running OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol, for about $40,000 in API charges.
